data.languages#Languages:
23 lexers. Each is a transcription of the reference rouge 5.0.0 gem’s own lexer source, and each is validated byte-for-byte against HTML produced by that gem: every corpus file in testdata/ is highlighted by both and the output compared exactly.
Language Tags C c C++ cpp, c++ COBOL cobol CSS css diff diff, patch, udiff Fortran fortran Go go, golang Hashicorp Configuration Language hcl HTML html Java java JavaScript javascript, js JSON json Markdown markdown, md, mkd PHP php, php3, php4, php5 Plain Text plaintext, text Python python, py Ruby ruby, rb Rust rust, rs (+ the six rust-skeptic aliases) shell shell, bash, zsh, ksh, sh SQL sql Terraform terraform, tf TeX latex, tex, TeX, LaTeX YAML yaml, yml Where a lexer is not byte-identical, the module says so
The README carries a documented simplifications section listing every deviation from the gem and the measurement behind it — for example that the gem’s ^ and lookbehind assertions do not constrain where it evaluates them, so three rules drop them; and that HCL’s here-document rule is not transcribed because the gem’s own rule ordering makes it unreachable. Nothing is left to be discovered by surprise.

data.rouge#rouge: Rouge/Pygments-class lexers that tokenize source and emit highlighted HTML.
data.use#Use: import "github.com/go-rouge/rouge" html, err := rouge.Highlight(`puts "hello"`, "ruby", "html") // => puts "hello" lex := rouge.FindLexer("rb") // by tag or alias, case-insensitive lex = rouge.Guess(src) // content sniff; never nil (PlainText fallback) toks := lex.Lex(src) // []TokenValue{Token, Value} page := rouge.WrapHTML(rouge.HTMLFormatter{}.Format(toks)) The CSS short-codes are the gem’s own (k, s, c, nf, …), so any stylesheet written for Ruby rouge — or for Pygments — styles this output unchanged.
